basis: two ways of light and darkness
note: The commentary contrasts a guided way with a path of straying; Barnabas introduces two ways, one of light and one of darkness, extending that moral division in early Christian instruction.
The commentary names a group defined by straying; Barnabas details the way of darkness through its destructive practices, making the wrong path concrete.

basis: Way of Life and Way of Death
note: The commentary's road splits between a favored and a ruined group; this early Christian teaching opens with two ways, one of life and one of death.

basis: way of light and way of darkness
note: The commentary's found path is associated with brightness and its lost path with dark affliction; Barnabas frames its ethical teaching as the two ways of light and darkness.

basis: cloud and sea in the exodus
note: The commentary begins its wrath scene with Israel rescued from an enemy; Paul recalls that all Israel passed under the cloud and through the sea, reframing the rescue for the church.
The commentary connects Israel's rebellion with wrath; Paul warns the congregation not to grumble as the wilderness generation did, whose people were destroyed.

basis: Israel's story written for later readers
note: The commentary uses Israel's provision and punishment to frame the path of the present reader; Paul explicitly says these events were written as instruction for those upon whom the ends of the ages have come.
The commentary recalls Israel's deliverance under Moses; Paul interprets the cloud and sea crossing as a baptism into Moses.
The commentary names manna as provision; Paul says all Israel ate the same spiritual food, reading the gift typologically.
The commentary's wilderness food is recalled by Paul as the spiritual food shared by the whole exodus generation, a Christian rereading of the manna gift.
The commentary recalls God's provision during the journey; Paul says Israel drank from a spiritual rock and identifies that rock with Christ.

basis: God not pleased in the wilderness
note: The commentary makes divine pleasure the opposite of wrath; Paul says God was not pleased with most of the manna-fed generation and their bodies were scattered in the wilderness.
The commentary reads Israel's food and transgression as a warning; Paul tells the church that these events became examples so they would not desire evil as Israel did.
The commentary uses the calf to connect provision, idolatry, and wrath; Paul invokes the calf tradition to warn his readers not to be idolaters.
The commentary's two faces foreshadow differing final bodily states; Paul contrasts a body sown in dishonor and weakness with one raised in glory and power.

basis: praise given when the Lord comes
note: The commentary glosses hamd as praise and approval and names the day of recompense; Paul says the Lord's coming reveals hidden motives and each person then receives praise from God.

basis: praise from God at final judgment
note: The commentary opens its contrast with hamd, praise and approval, and names a day of reckoning; Paul locates each person's praise from God at the Lord's coming judgment.
The commentary distinguishes a guided way from straying; John says claiming fellowship while walking in darkness is falsehood.
The commentary connects the favored way with a visible sign of well-being; John says walking in the light brings fellowship and cleansing from sin.

basis: walking in light, fellowship, and cleansing
note: The commentary says the favored path is traveled with companions and ends in forgiveness; John links walking in light to fellowship with one another and cleansing from sin.

basis: confession followed by forgiveness and cleansing
note: The commentary's grace side includes forgiveness after wrongdoing; John says confession is met by God's faithful forgiveness and cleansing from unrighteousness.

basis: darkness blinds the eyes and obscures the way
note: The commentary's hostile face includes disturbed eyes and its theological result is waylessness; this verse says hatred leaves a person in darkness, blinded in the eyes, ignorant of where to go.
The commentary says a group receives favor while another strays; Peter says those once not a people have become God's people and those without mercy have received mercy.

basis: formerly without mercy, now receiving mercy
note: The commentary's two groups are distinguished by bestowed ni'ma versus divine disfavor; Peter contrasts being not a people and without mercy with becoming God's people and receiving mercy.
The commentary names the favored as a gathered community on a path; Peter describes a chosen people called out of darkness into God's marvelous light.

basis: chosen people called from darkness to light
note: The commentary's favored community is both chosen and visibly luminous; Peter calls a chosen people out of darkness into God's marvelous light.
The commentary says the face carries the sign of wrath or favor; Peter says the Lord's eyes are on the righteous and his face is against those who do evil, applying the contrast to Christian conduct.

basis: the Lord's eyes on righteous and face against evil
note: The commentary contrasts a favored group with those under divine disfavor and makes face and eye central; Peter juxtaposes the Lord's eyes upon the righteous with the Lord's face against evildoers.

basis: glory's Spirit resting upon the reviled
note: The commentary's favor is something that descends upon a group; Peter calls reviled believers blessed because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon them.
The commentary juxtaposes wrath with a saving, favorable end; Paul describes Jesus as the one who rescues believers from the wrath that is coming.
The commentary emphasizes wrath as something that comes upon a group without naming its agent in the Arabic passive; Paul uses the closely parallel image that wrath has come upon them.

basis: the day does not overtake children of light
note: The commentary pairs the judgment day with faces that reveal each group's outcome; Paul says believers are not in darkness for the day to overtake them like a thief.
The commentary divides the guided from the straying; Paul calls the community children of light and children of day, not of night or darkness.

basis: appointed for salvation rather than wrath
note: The commentary divides humanity between a gift-bearing and a wrath-bearing outcome; Paul explicitly says God has not appointed believers for wrath but for obtaining salvation.
The commentary says favor and judgment are visible on faces; Paul describes people with unveiled faces being transformed as they behold the Lord's glory.
The commentary turns divine favor into a face's condition; Paul extends the Moses image to believers whose unveiled faces are being transformed into the same image.
The commentary's bright face is set in a Moses-and-wrath complex; Paul rereads Moses' radiant face as the visible glory of the old covenant.
The commentary links blessing with a radiant face; Paul locates the knowledge of God's glory in the face of Jesus Christ.

basis: light of God's glory in Christ's face
note: The commentary makes divine favor visible on the face; Paul says God has shone in hearts to give the light of the knowledge of God's glory in the face of Christ.

basis: each appears before the judgment seat
note: The commentary names the day of recompense; Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat and receive according to what they did.
The commentary opens the scene with divine pleasure and closes it with judgment; Paul says his aim is to please the Lord before describing the judgment seat in the next verse.

basis: patience seeking repentance rather than perishing
note: The commentary contrasts a wrathful fall with repentance and a found way; Peter explains divine patience as not wishing people to perish but to come to repentance.
The commentary names prophets, martyrs, and the righteous as companions; Paul says Christ comes to be glorified among his saints and marveled at by those who believed.

basis: relief for the afflicted at revelation
note: The commentary sets wrath against the reward of the guided; Paul says the afflicted will receive relief when Jesus is revealed from heaven.
The commentary names wrath coming upon a group; Paul describes punishment for those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel when the Lord is revealed.

basis: darkness falling on a judgment-blinded eye
note: The commentary gives anger a bodily eye-image and says something comes upon its recipient; Paul announces the Lord's hand against Elymas, after which mist and darkness immediately fall on him and he seeks a guide.

basis: eyes opened, darkness turned to light, forgiveness
note: The commentary joins seeing, guidance, repentance, and favor; Paul's commission is to open eyes, turn people from darkness to light, and give forgiveness and an inheritance.
The commentary makes repentance and a turn toward right guidance the way out of wrath; Peter calls hearers to repent and turn so that sins may be wiped out.
The commentary's en'amte alayhim has an explicit giver and a group upon whom favor rests; Acts says great grace was upon all the witness-bearing community.
The commentary treats the face as a bearer of a person's spiritual condition; Stephen's opponents see his face as that of an angel while he testifies before judgment.
The commentary recalls the calf and Moses' anger; Stephen recounts Israel making the calf and offering sacrifice to the work of their hands.
The commentary's calf episode is retold here with Israel making the calf, offering sacrifice to it, and rejoicing in what their hands made.
The commentary links the calf with divine wrath; Stephen interprets Israel's idolatry as the point at which God turned away and gave them over to heavenly worship.

basis: share the inheritance of the saints in light
note: The commentary names prophets and righteous among the favored; Paul gives thanks that believers are qualified to share the inheritance of the saints in light.

basis: transferred from darkness into the Son's kingdom
note: The commentary contrasts the guided with those who stray; Paul says God rescued people from darkness and transferred them into the kingdom of his beloved Son, where there is redemption and forgiveness.

basis: rescue from darkness into a kingdom
note: The commentary's divine deliverance moves people away from the lost side; Paul says the Father rescues people from the domain of darkness and transfers them to the Son's kingdom.

basis: eyes of the heart enlightened for hope
note: The commentary makes the eye's condition carry guidance and favor; Paul prays for enlightened heart-eyes so believers know the hope of calling and inheritance.
The commentary's passive group is described as those upon whom wrath has fallen; Paul calls people by nature children of wrath, naming a condition before the following mercy.
The commentary ends with a collective named by wrath; Paul describes a former corporate condition as being children of wrath.
The commentary contrasts those under wrath with those who receive favor; Paul turns immediately to God's great mercy and love for people.
The commentary does not end at wrath but gives forgiveness a path onward; Paul immediately counters the prior wrath condition with God's rich mercy and great love.
The commentary sets wrath against the outcome of favor; Paul says people dead in trespasses are made alive with Christ by grace.

basis: Christ shining on one who rises
note: The commentary's eschatological face is lit after a fall or deathlike state; the cited hymn commands the sleeper to rise from the dead so Christ will shine upon that person.

basis: once darkness, now light; walk as light
note: The commentary joins the path to faces that shine or darken; Paul says the hearers were once darkness but are now light in the Lord and must walk as children of light.

basis: formerly darkness, now light, therefore walk
note: The commentary's contrast joins identity, light, and a road; Paul says believers were darkness but are now light in the Lord and commands them to walk as children of light.
The commentary connects praise with approval and divine pleasure; Paul asks whether he seeks human approval or God's and says pleasing people would make him no servant of Christ.

basis: Christ becoming a curse for others
note: The commentary contrasts a group under anger with a group granted favor; Paul presents Christ as becoming a curse in order to redeem others from the law's curse, a different distributive account of adverse judgment.
The commentary names prophets, truth-affirmers, martyrs, and the righteous as companions; Hebrews gathers faithful exemplars who were commended but had not yet received what was promised.
The commentary describes the favored as companions on one path; Hebrews says the earlier faithful are not made complete apart from the later community, extending the company across generations.
The commentary sets divine pleasure against wrath; Hebrews says faith is necessary to please God and that those who approach him must trust that he rewards those who seek him.

basis: cloud of witnesses and shared race
note: The commentary calls the favored a group walking together; Hebrews pictures a cloud of witnesses surrounding the hearers as they run the race set before them.

basis: cloud of witnesses and a race to run
note: The commentary's favored way is a shared route with exemplary companions; Hebrews places believers within a cloud of witnesses and tells them to run the course set before them.

basis: assembly of the righteous in heaven
note: The commentary lists prophets, truth-affirmers, martyrs, and righteous companions; Hebrews describes the assembly of the firstborn and the spirits of righteous people made complete.
The commentary ends with those who lose the path and those guided; Hebrews quotes God's complaint that the wilderness generation always goes astray in heart and has not known his ways.
The commentary binds divine anger to losing the right path; this wilderness interpretation says God was angry because the generation went astray in heart and did not know his ways.

basis: God's anger with the wilderness generation
note: The commentary says wrath comes upon a group after rebellion; Hebrews asks with whom God was angry for forty years and answers with those who sinned.

basis: angry forty years and fallen bodies
note: The commentary calls wrath a fall; Hebrews explicitly asks whether God was angry with those whose bodies fell in the wilderness.
The commentary ties the day and the path to each group's end; Hebrews says the disobedient were barred by oath from entering God's rest.
The commentary's lost group does not reach the guided path's end; Hebrews concludes that the wilderness generation could not enter because of unbelief.
The commentary links the favored with prostration and weeping; Hebrews describes Jesus offering prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears, tying bodily humility to being heard.
The commentary describes benefaction as coming upon the favored; James says every good and perfect gift comes down from above from the Father of lights.

basis: human anger does not make justice
note: The commentary opposes wrath to favor and the straight way; James says human anger does not produce God's righteousness, an ethical warning about anger's outcome.
The commentary's wrath-side loses the way and falls; Jesus's paired saying makes the night-walker stumble because light is not in that person.
The commentary joins correct guidance to light and an unfallen walk; Jesus says that a person walking in the day does not stumble because that person sees the world's light.
The commentary says anger and error lose the road; Jesus says one walking in darkness does not know where one is going.
The commentary asks whose judgment one approves and sets God's favor against anger; John says some loved human glory more than God's glory, explaining their refusal to confess Jesus.

basis: judgment as loving darkness rather than light
note: The commentary's two groups end in luminous or darkened conditions; Jesus explains judgment through the light's arrival and evildoers' love of darkness.

basis: doing truth and coming to light
note: The commentary's favorable side joins right action to a found way; the one doing truth comes to the light so deeds can be seen as done in God.
The commentary's phrase describes people with wrath upon them; John says God's wrath remains on the one who disobeys the Son, alongside the alternative of eternal life.

basis: the dead hear and come out
note: The commentary names the day of recompense for groups with different outcomes; Jesus speaks of the hour when all in the tombs hear his voice and come out.
The commentary divides the judged into opposite destinations; Jesus says those who did good rise to life and those who did evil rise to judgment.

basis: manna interpreted through bread from heaven
note: The commentary recalls manna as a gift to Israel; Jesus' hearers cite the ancestors eating manna and receiving bread from heaven, opening a Christian dispute over who gives the true bread.
The commentary says God bestowed wilderness food; Jesus corrects the claim that Moses gave the bread and identifies the Father as giver of the true bread from heaven.
The commentary recalls manna as provision; Jesus identifies himself as the bread of life and promises that the one coming to him will not hunger.
The commentary places food beside the final day and its outcomes; Jesus says the ancestors ate manna in the wilderness and died, distinguishing provision from everlasting life.
The commentary presents manna as a remembered divine favor; Jesus contrasts that wilderness manna with death, so the Christian discourse assigns the old gift a deliberately limited result.
The commentary connects bestowed favor with the guided path's end; Jesus says the bread from heaven can be eaten so that the eater will not die.

basis: living bread for the world's life
note: The commentary recalls God's gift of food to Israel; Jesus calls himself living bread and says the bread he gives is for the life of the world.

basis: living bread from heaven gives life
note: The commentary's descending provision is manna; Jesus identifies himself as the living bread come down from heaven, turning the exodus image toward his life-giving claim.

basis: Jesus as exodus deliverer and judge
note: The commentary recalls God delivering Israel and then judging rebellion; Jude's text names Jesus as the one who saved a people from Egypt and later destroyed unbelievers, a Christological retelling of the scene.
The commentary describes favor as softening the face and lighting its surface; Zechariah's song says God's mercy brings a dawn from on high to visit the people.

basis: tender mercy and dawn from on high
note: The commentary joins divine favor to the image of a day and light; Zechariah grounds the rising dawn in the tender mercy of God before its guidance imagery in the next verse.

basis: light guides feet into peace's way
note: The commentary joins visible favor to a shared path; Zechariah says the dawn shines on those in darkness and guides their feet into the way of peace.

basis: light and feet guided into peace
note: The commentary puts the favorable face and the right road together; Zechariah's hymn says divine dawn shines on those in darkness and guides their feet into the way of peace.
The commentary turns favor into an eye's state; Jesus calls the eyes blessed that see what prophets and kings desired to see.

The commentary names prophets among the favored and contrasts them with the lost; Jesus describes people seeing Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the prophets in God's kingdom while they themselves are cast out.

basis: gathered company at the kingdom table
note: The commentary describes the favored as companions on a path; Jesus pictures people coming from every direction to recline together in God's kingdom.

basis: lost and found at a father's welcome
note: The commentary contrasts being lost with a forgiven return to the way; the father identifies the returned son as formerly lost and now found and celebrates him.
The commentary names those who stray and asks for guidance; Jesus depicts a shepherd going after one lost sheep until he finds it, turning the straying image into a search for restoration.
The commentary says some receive forgiveness rather than wrath; Jesus says heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents, interpreting recovery of the lost as joy rather than rejection.

The commentary recalls favored people falling in worship and weeping; Luke depicts a woman weeping at Jesus' feet, wetting and wiping them, an embodied act of grief and devotion that Jesus receives in a forgiveness scene.
The commentary contrasts the faces of two groups on the day; Jesus says the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom after the wicked are removed.
The commentary's final-day favored faces shine; Jesus says the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom.

basis: Jesus' face shining like the sun
note: The commentary gives the blessed face a luminous aspect; the transfiguration states that Jesus' face shone like the sun, within a scene of divine approval.

basis: well-done approval and entry into joy
note: The commentary glosses hamd as approval or being pleased; the master praises the faithful servant and admits that servant into the master's joy.
The commentary distinguishes those receiving favor from those under wrath at the day; the Son of Man invites those at his right hand as blessed by the Father into the prepared kingdom.
The commentary's favored group receives a divine gift and shares a destination; the king calls the blessed to inherit the kingdom prepared for them.

basis: cursed ones depart from the judge
note: The commentary uses a passive label for those upon whom wrath has fallen; here the king explicitly addresses the cursed and sends them away, making the judge's agency overt.
The commentary's second group bears divine wrath and abasement; the king's opposite verdict sends the cursed away to the prepared fire.
The commentary's day carries two opposite outcomes; Matthew closes the judgment scene with punishment for one group and eternal life for the other.
The commentary enumerates prophets and martyrs among the favored companions; Jesus tells the persecuted to rejoice because their reward is great and the prophets were persecuted before them.

basis: a face can be deliberately disfigured
note: The commentary reads faces as signs of inward outcomes; Jesus warns that hypocrites disfigure their faces to display fasting, showing that a visible religious face can be staged for human notice.

The commentary makes a face show an inward religious condition and begins with praise; Jesus criticizes fasters who disfigure their faces to be seen by people, distinguishing their received human reward from divine regard.
The commentary gives the face a role in visible favor or wrath; Jesus tells the fasting person to wash and anoint the face so devotion is not performed for human observers.

basis: anointed head and washed face before the Father
note: The commentary's favorable face is not merely a legal verdict; Jesus tells secret fasters to anoint the head and wash the face so the Father, rather than observers, sees and rewards.
The commentary says faces carry a visible mark of judgment; Jesus contrasts public appearance with the Father who sees what is hidden and rewards accordingly.

basis: the healthy eye filling the body with light
note: The commentary's favorable eye is calm and bright; Jesus uses a healthy eye as the condition by which the whole body is full of light.
The commentary's adverse face includes an afflicted eye and dark covering; Jesus's paired image makes the bad eye produce darkness throughout the body.

basis: the broad road leads to destruction
note: The commentary ends with a guided path opposed to those who stray; Jesus contrasts the broad road that leads to destruction and the many who enter it.
The commentary's wrath side is a lost way and a fall; Jesus describes a broad way that leads to destruction and has many travelers.

basis: the narrow path leads to life
note: The commentary asks to be guided to the straight path; Jesus says the narrow gate and hard way lead to life and are found by few.
The commentary's favored side is a found path; Jesus contrasts it with a narrow way that leads to life and is found by few.

basis: company with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
note: The commentary says the favored road is shared with exemplary companions; Jesus depicts many joining the patriarchs at the kingdom meal.
The commentary gives the adverse group a dark, humiliated bodily condition; Jesus contrasts the kingdom meal with expulsion into outer darkness, weeping, and gnashing.

basis: God works for his good pleasure
note: The commentary says the favored gift is actively bestowed; Paul says God works within the community both to will and to work for his good pleasure.

basis: shining lights among a crooked generation
note: The commentary contrasts the favored path with those who stray and says faces may shine; Paul calls believers blameless children of God who shine like lights in a crooked generation.
The commentary makes final grace visible in bodily appearance; Paul expects Christ to transform the lowly body into conformity with his glorious body.
The commentary's golden-calf warning culminates in divine anger; Revelation gives beast worshipers wine of God's wrath, a later apocalyptic pairing of idolatry and wrath.

basis: blessed dead whose deeds follow them
note: The commentary names martyrs among those receiving favor; Revelation calls the dead who die in the Lord blessed, says they rest from toil, and says their deeds follow them.
The commentary turns the calf's idolatry into a wrath-bearing fate visible on the face; Revelation marks beast-worshipers on forehead or hand before announcing their judgment.
The commentary recalls manna as an indicator of divine favor; Revelation promises hidden manna specifically to the one who conquers, relocating wilderness provision into an eschatological reward.
The commentary names the day of recompense; Revelation depicts the dead standing before the throne while books are opened and they are judged by their deeds.

basis: book of life and the opposite end
note: The commentary divides groups by their final outcome; Revelation says those not found in the book of life are thrown into the lake of fire.
The commentary includes martyrs among the favored companions; Revelation pictures those slain for their testimony seated on thrones, given judgment, and reigning with Christ.

basis: God's glory as the city's light
note: The commentary's blessed final side is luminous; Revelation says the eschatological city needs neither sun nor moon because God's glory gives it light.

basis: conqueror inherits and belongs to God
note: The commentary's favorable side receives a gift and shares a divine companionship; Revelation promises inheritance and a God-child relation to the one who conquers.

basis: lake of fire for the unfaithful
note: The commentary's adverse group has an eschatological judgment distinct from the favored group; Revelation supplies the opposed fate for the cowardly, faithless, and idolaters.
The commentary contrasts wrath with favor and the guided with the lost; Revelation's final city has no more curse, and God's servants worship there.
The commentary says faces display the outcome of judgment; Revelation describes the servants seeing God's face and bearing his name on their foreheads.
The commentary's favorable final side has a transformed face; Revelation's servants see God's face and bear his name on their foreheads.

basis: God's light on the final servants
note: The commentary's bright face belongs to a final favored community; Revelation says the Lord God will give light to his servants, with no more night.

basis: eye salve, white garments, and exposed shame
note: The commentary's two faces include afflicted eyes and visible favor; the risen Christ counsels the blind, naked church to obtain eye salve for sight and white garments to cover shame.

basis: elders fall and worship in praise
note: The commentary's chosen company prostrates in praise; the elders fall before the enthroned one, worship, and cast down their crowns.

basis: faces hidden from the enthroned one
note: The commentary reads the face as bearing the mark of wrath; Revelation's rulers and people ask to be hidden from the face of the enthroned one and from the Lamb's anger.

basis: hiding from the enthroned face and the Lamb's wrath
note: The commentary makes wrath and a face inseparable images; those facing judgment seek to hide from the face of the enthroned one and from the Lamb's wrath.
The commentary calls the day the bearer of judgment; Revelation's terrified speakers ask who can stand when the great day of divine and Lamb's wrath has arrived.
The commentary's yawm carries the two outcomes; Revelation calls the crisis the great day of their wrath and asks who can stand.

basis: all heavenly attendants fall on their faces
note: The commentary joins the favored assembly to prostration; angels, elders, and living creatures fall before the throne on their faces and worship God.

basis: no hunger, thirst, scorching, or heat
note: The commentary begins with wilderness food and ends with bodily marked destinies; Revelation's favorable multitude will neither hunger nor thirst and will not be struck by scorching heat.

basis: the Lamb guides to living springs
note: The commentary says the favored are guided on a path and their faces show the outcome; Revelation's Lamb shepherds the multitude, guides them to springs of living water, and wipes away every tear.

basis: guided to living water and tears wiped
note: The commentary couples a gifted community with guidance and a relaxed face; the Lamb shepherds the multitude to springs of living water and God wipes every tear from their eyes.
The commentary describes the favored as a community on one path; Revelation shows an uncountable multitude from every nation standing together before the throne and the Lamb.
The commentary calls wrath something that descends upon people; Paul describes God's wrath as being revealed from heaven against ungodliness and unrighteousness.
The commentary's rida-ghadaab contrast is expressed as two divine dispositions; Paul asks readers to consider God's kindness and severity, with continuance in kindness opposed to being cut off.
The commentary sets two groups under judgment; Paul names glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good, Jew first and Greek as well.

basis: glory, honor, and peace for doing good
note: The commentary's favorable side receives an approving divine outcome; Paul promises glory, honor, and peace to everyone who works good, against the wrath named in the same argument.
The commentary describes hamd as approval; Paul says the true inward Jew receives praise from God rather than from human beings.
The commentary names the day that bears wrath and recompense; Paul calls it a day of wrath and the revelation of God's righteous judgment.

basis: day of wrath and righteous judgment
note: The commentary calls yawm the days carrying punishment and forgiveness; Paul speaks of a day of wrath and revelation of God's righteous judgment.

basis: glory, honor, and life for the patient
note: The commentary contrasts wrath with the outcome of the guided; Paul sets eternal life and glory for those who persevere in doing good against the day of judgment.
The commentary's favor side includes faithful action and an ultimate outcome; Paul names eternal life for those persevering in good work and seeking glory, honor, and incorruptibility.

basis: wrath for those who reject truth
note: The commentary distinguishes the wrath-struck from the guided; Paul describes wrath and fury for those who reject truth and follow unrighteousness.
The commentary makes wrath the adverse outcome of rebellion; Paul sets wrath and anger on those who reject truth and obey unrighteousness.
The commentary contrasts those upon whom wrath falls with the forgiven; Paul says those justified by Christ's blood will be saved from wrath through him.

basis: justification and rescue from wrath through Christ
note: The commentary describes repentance, faith, good action, and guidance as the route beyond wrath; Paul frames rescue from wrath through Christ's blood, a distinct Christian account of the saving transition.

The commentary contrasts a granted blessing with wrath falling on another group; Paul speaks of vessels of wrath and God's patience toward them, a close but not identical account of agency and judgment.

basis: vessels of mercy prepared for glory
note: The commentary contrasts the wrath-struck with those granted favor; Paul pairs vessels of wrath with vessels of mercy prepared for glory, making the two-group contrast explicit.
The commentary's two groups have opposed paths, visual states, and ends; the Community Rule's two-spirits instruction systematically assigns light and darkness, conduct, and judgment to opposed lots.
The commentary distinguishes two groups by the path they follow; the Community Rule describes opposing spirits that direct human conduct and lead to different outcomes at God's visitation.

basis: light, peace, and life of truth
note: The commentary's favored group walks a guided way and bears a softened face; the Community Rule associates the spirit of truth with enlightenment, peace, and life, giving a Jewish sectarian account of the favorable path.
The commentary treats rida and anger as opposed divine dispositions; the high-priest tradition has God speak of mercy overcoming anger, an interpretive attempt to hold the opposition together.

basis: the two ways of life and death
note: The commentary closes by distinguishing groups through the path they follow; the Didache opens its teaching with the way of life and the way of death and their sharply different outcomes.

basis: good eye, good companion, good way
note: The commentary reads the favored path as one walked with good companions and a settled eye; this mishnah deliberately pairs a good eye and good companion with a good way, then supplies their evil counterparts.
The commentary describes anger as boiling blood and desire for revenge; Avot defines the mighty person as one who conquers his own inclination, redirecting strength toward self-command.

basis: anger measured by capacity to reconcile
note: The commentary sets anger against pleasure and describes its bodily face; Avot distinguishes temperaments by how readily a person becomes angry and how readily they are appeased.
The commentary treats anger and rida as opposed dispositions; this temperament teaching distinguishes people by being easy or hard to anger and easy or hard to appease.

basis: blessing God for evil as for good
note: The commentary begins with hamd and its opposition to blame while contrasting ni'ma and wrath; this mishnah requires blessing God for adverse events as for good, changing how praise relates to an unwelcome divine event.
The commentary needs the relation of calf-wrath to forgiveness; this rabbinic reading makes Exodus 34's attributes a liturgical pattern by which Israel seeks pardon after sin.

basis: forgive a neighbor and be forgiven
note: The commentary opposes wrath to favor and pardon; Sirach says a person who forgives a neighbor's wrong can seek forgiveness for their own sins, linking restraint of anger with receiving mercy.
The commentary makes wrath a consequential state; Sirach asks the angry person to remember death and the commandments, then relinquish enmity.

The commentary contrasts an angry, fallen face with favor; Onkelos interprets God's answer to Cain in terms of forgiveness if he does well, making the face scene a question of repentance and restored standing.

basis: faces down and confession after divine fire
note: The commentary associates prostration and praise with a divinely favored manifestation; after the fire, the people fall on their faces and confess that YHWH is God.

basis: favor sought and a no-longer-sad face
note: The commentary makes favor visible in a changed face; after Hannah asks to find favor and receives Eli's word of peace, she eats and her face is no longer as before.
The commentary says benefaction cools the eye and recalls food given in the wilderness; Jonathan eats honey and his eyes brighten, a concrete bodily sign of refreshment after nourishment.

basis: faces to the ground in praise
note: The commentary depicts the favored, guided people prostrating and praises God; Israel sees divine glory and fire, bows with faces to the ground, worships, and gives thanks.
The commentary says the day carries both wrath and deliverance; Amos warns those expecting the Lord's day that it will be darkness rather than light, a direct reversal of presumed favor.
The commentary places two groups under the judgment of the day; Daniel describes some awakening to everlasting life and others to shame and everlasting contempt.
The commentary describes the final day as two visibly different destinies; Daniel's resurrection vision divides the sleepers between everlasting life and everlasting contempt.
The commentary says the day's outcome appears on faces; Daniel says the wise and those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the brightness of the sky and stars.
The commentary's favored faces are luminous; Daniel says the wise, including those who turn many to righteousness, will shine like the expanse and stars.

basis: judgment changing a king's facial color
note: The commentary reads judgment in the body's face; after the divine writing appears, Belshazzar's facial color changes and his body is visibly shaken.
The commentary names a day of recompense for two groups; Daniel's vision shows the court seated and the books opened before the beast is judged.

basis: shame of face under sin and judgment
